paras: The Richmond, Texas, train assault was an attack in the summer of 1900 on Black passengers on a Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway train bound for Houston, allegedly by drunken white men including J. B. and William Wheat. It became known through damage suits by Black plaintiffs that together sought more than $95,000.
Joseph Parker of Houston, by his petition, had married Sally Jones at Richmond and was taking her home by train, "a few weeks" before the suits of August 1.

White men in the Richmond waiting room for Black passengers, all apparently drunk, cursed Parker at the ticket window before his wife. The San Antonio Daily Light described them as "waiters, most of them intoxicated," the Wheats among them. They then entered the Black coach, where, the petition charged, they terrorized the passengers with drawn sixshooters and injured some.

Appeals to the conductor brought no protection; he moved the Black passengers to the smoking compartment, where the whites followed, or, in the Light's version, "was afraid to do anything." Near Blodgett the Wheats allegedly threw out Parker's grip, holding $200 and a $50 watch, and the couple's hats. Another passenger, Jim Mitchell, was said to have been driven insane, probably fatally, by the Wheats.

Parker and Richard Jones, with substantially the same complaint, each sued the railway and the Wheats for $20,000 at Houston; Mitchell's family had sued earlier. The Light reported the Wheats under arrest at Richmond; no trial or verdict was found.

Two white Texas dailies carried the story, both drawing on the petitions. The Houston Daily Post ran it in court news on August 2 as "Two More Heavy Suits," "All Brought by Negroes Who Allege that They Were Mistreated," attributing each charge to the petitions. The Light's Sunday special of August 5 was jocular, calling the episode a "Lively Train Experience" and the Wheats "Two Wild and Woolly Texans" who "Woke Up Things" in the coach.
The papers differ on the Mitchell suits, $55,400 in the Post and $50,400 by his mother and sister in the Light, and on Jones's filing date.

reader.title: Richmond, Texas, train assault
bases: A drunken party of white men, among them J. B. and William Wheat, allegedly invaded the coach for Black passengers with drawn pistols, injured some passengers, threw property from the train and left one man insane; no one was killed (A1, A2).

Two separately written Texas reports agree on the core event and add different details (A1, A2), though both rest on the plaintiffs' petitions; the Light's report that the Wheats were under arrest at Richmond is the only non-petition fact (A2).

accounts.label: Parker's petition, as summarized by the Houston Post
accounts.gist: Drunken whites abused Parker at the Richmond ticket window, boarded the Black coach, terrorized passengers with drawn sixshooters and injured some; the conductor moved the Black passengers to the smoker, where the whites followed; near Blodgett the Wheats threw Parker's baggage off.

accounts.label: Houston special to the San Antonio Light
accounts.gist: A party of mostly intoxicated waiters including the Wheats threw hats and a grip from the train; the Black passengers fled; the conductor was afraid to act; Mitchell was made insane by the Wheats; the Wheats were under arrest.

framing.detail: The Houston Daily Post's court column headlined 'Two More Heavy Suits' and attributed every charge to the petitions, emphasizing the sums claimed.
The San Antonio Daily Light reported the allegations plainly but headlined them as a 'Lively Train Experience' by 'Two Wild and Woolly Texans' who 'Woke Up Things' in the coach.

versions.value: $50,400, filed by Mitchell's mother and sister

conflicts.note: Both papers give a total near $95,000; the Post's figures ($40,000 + $55,400) are internally consistent with its 'over $95,000'.

info: On a train 'a few weeks' before Aug. 1, 1900; exact date not given
Began at the depot in Richmond, Texas; on a Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway train bound for Houston; baggage thrown off near Blodgett
Joseph Parker and his bride (Sally Jones), Richard Jones, and Jim (J.) Mitchell, all described as colored; other Black passengers
None; no accusation against the Black passengers is reported
J. B. and William Wheat and a party of white men, described as waiters, most of them intoxicated
Damage suits: Parker and Jones $20,000 each against the railway and the Wheats; Mitchell suits $55,400 (A1) or $50,400 (A2); total over $95,000. No outcome reported
